Bare except Exception is intentional for a fail-soft fetch helper. The goal is that _run_issue_linker always completes and never propagates errors from the issue fetch to the caller. exc_info=True preserves the full traceback in the log, and the same (unavailable) sentinel is the correct degraded behavior regardless of the error type.

The async cancellation scope concern is acknowledged but the current code is safe: _fetch_open_issues passes timeout=15 to subprocess.run, so the thread always unblocks within 15 seconds. Adding an anyio cancellation scope would be defensive over-engineering that adds complexity without benefit given the existing subprocess timeout. A code comment was added in the original implementation noting this design choice.

— `max()` is intentional: all agents share the same `<symbol-context>` block injected once, so each agent's `context_tokens_used` is the same value. Using `max()` avoids double-counting. See dispatch.py comment: 'all agents share the same context block so only the max is meaningful'.
— same rationale as F2: `max()` on a single-element generator simply returns that element; the `default=0` handles the empty-results case. This is correct behavior.

— `diff_path` is always defined before the `try` block: the `with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(..., delete=False) as f: diff_path = Path(f.name)` context manager exits cleanly before the `try` begins. If the NamedTemporaryFile constructor itself raises, `diff_path` is never set and the `finally` is never reached — there is nothing to clean up. The `finally` path is correct.

— this is a memory-bank analysis script, not production code. Errors are printed in `main()` via the top-level `asyncio.run()` call. Wrapping `fetch_diff()` internal errors in additional context is unnecessary for a one-off evaluation harness.

— `run_analyzers` is intentionally fail-soft by design: a single analyzer crashing should never abort the whole review. The same behavior exists in the bash engine. Adding a sentinel return type would break the caller's interface and add complexity for a scenario (MemoryError, SystemExit inside a subprocess wrapper) that the OS-level process boundary already contains. The warning to stderr is the appropriate signal.

capture_output=True buffers all subprocess output in memory — there is no truncation. The concern about 'very large shellcheck output' is moot: subprocess.run with capture_output buffers the complete stdout regardless of size.

Path resolution uses Path(f).is_file() which is consistent with the bash wrapper behavior. Shell file paths in CI are always absolute (set by review.sh from git diff output). A CWD-relative path would only occur if a caller constructs ChangedFiles manually with relative paths, which no production caller does.
The 200-char stderr truncation is intentional and matches the existing bash-path pattern in _run_analyzer. This is a cosmetic cap on warning output length, not a loss of actionable information.
returncode=1 is the expected exit code when ruff finds violations (same as shellcheck); returning [] on exit codes other than 0 and 1 is the correct error gate, matching the bash wrapper behavior

The REQUEST_CHANGES-to-COMMENT degrade path does not need an equivalent correction note: unlike the APPROVE branch, the REQUEST_CHANGES review body renders the exact same generic "## AI Review Findings" heading as a plain COMMENT (see `_render_review_body`, the "COMMENT with findings or REQUEST_CHANGES" branch) — it never claims changes were formally requested anywhere in the text. GitHub's own "Changes requested" banner is metadata on the review event, not body text, so there is no false claim in the body left uncorrected when this degrades. The event mismatch itself is still surfaced via the generic event-comparison warning in reporting.py's emit_review_result/write_step_summary, which fires for any intended-vs-posted event divergence, not just APPROVE. This was independently verified by two review agents during the PR's pre-push /comprehensive-review pass.

not applicable — policy_gate_satisfied deliberately checks config.review_mode (the run's actual effective mode, which can come from an explicit /ai-pr-review review-full override), not the matched policy's own declared mode. policy_satisfies() checks resolve_policy(policy_file, ran_policy_name).review_mode instead — the matched policy's own mode. These answer different questions and aren't interchangeable: a PR reviewed via an explicit full-mode override, whose matched policy is a lower quick-based tier, would stop satisfying a merge-gate requirement if this were replaced with a call to policy_satisfies(), exactly the case the comment directly above this code documents.

subprocess.run here is called with a list argv and the default shell=False, so target_files entries are passed as literal argv elements to execve — never interpreted by a shell. There is no command-injection path regardless of file content; a dash-leading filename is separately guarded by the preceding `--` argument. This is the same longstanding pattern used by every sibling native analyzer (shellcheck, ruff, checkov, tflint, etc.) in this codebase.
